title: Rolling updates: the arithmetic of maxSurge and maxUnavailable
summary: Compute the Pod-count limits of a rolling update from the manifest, and use them to predict how a rollout proceeds or stalls.
prereqText: From the previous lesson: a template change creates a new ReplicaSet which is scaled up while the old one is scaled down.

blocks.html: You push a new image of a web service with 3 replicas. You expect Pods to be swapped one at a time. But someone asks: can the cluster ever run 4 Pods at once during the update? Can it ever run only 2? Those are not trivia; they are capacity and cost questions during every deploy, and they decide whether a bad version can take your service down. Both answers come from two fields in the manifest.

blocks.prompt: A Deployment has replicas: 3 and the default rolling-update settings (maxSurge 25%, maxUnavailable 25%). What is the most Pods that may exist, and the fewest that must be available, during an update?
options: Up to 4 Pods; at least 3 available
Up to 3 Pods; at least 2 available
Up to 4 Pods; at least 2 available

feedback.1: Misconception: percentages round to nearest. Surge rounds up (25% of 3 = 0.75 → 1), so one extra Pod is allowed; the limit is not 3.
feedback.2: Misconception: both percentages round the same way. Unavailable rounds down (25% of 3 = 0.75 → 0), so zero Pods may be unavailable, and at least 3 must be available.

blocks.explanation: Surge: 25% of 3 = 0.75, rounded up to 1, so at most 3 + 1 = 4 Pods. Unavailable: 25% of 3 = 0.75, rounded down to 0, so at least 3 − 0 = 3 must be available. [source]

blocks.instructions: This is a model of the documented rules, not a cluster. First predict: with replicas 10, surge 30% and unavailable 20%, what are the max total Pods and minimum available? Then change the inputs. Find a setting where the percentages round to zero, and find the setting the docs say is not allowed.
blocks.debrief: You should have noticed that surge rounds up and unavailable rounds down, so with small replica counts a small percentage can still allow one extra Pod but zero unavailable. Setting both to zero is rejected by the rules: the controller would have no room to make progress.

config.title: Rolling-update limits
config.intro: Percentages follow the documented rounding: surge up, unavailable down.

interpret.html: Not a valid setting. The docs say maxUnavailable cannot be 0 if maxSurge is 0 (and vice versa): with no room to add or remove, no update could proceed.
Zero Pods may be unavailable. Capacity never drops, but every new Pod must become available before an old one can be removed.
Capacity can drop. A bad new version can reduce the number of serving Pods to the minimum shown.

assumptions: Models only the two documented limits; the order of individual controller steps is not modelled.
Uses the documented percentage rounding (surge up, unavailable down).

blocks.title: How the limits work
blocks.html:
With the default strategy, RollingUpdate, the controller scales the new ReplicaSet up and the old one down in steps. Two fields bound those steps. [source]

  • maxSurge: the most Pods that may exist above the desired count. An absolute number or a percentage; the number is computed by rounding up. Default 25%. So the ceiling is replicas + maxSurge.
  • maxUnavailable: the most desired Pods that may be unavailable. Percentage rounds down. Default 25%. So the floor is replicas − maxUnavailable available Pods.
  • Neither can be 0 if the other is 0.

Notice the word available. A Pod counts as available once it is ready; with minReadySeconds (default 0) it must stay ready that many seconds first. [source] The next lesson covers what "ready" means. For now take it as: the Pod is working and accepting traffic.

The rule that explains stalls. The controller may only remove an old Pod when doing so keeps available Pods at or above replicas − maxUnavailable, and may only create a new Pod when the total stays at or below replicas + maxSurge. If new Pods never become available, the available count never rises, so the controller runs out of permitted moves. That is a reading of the documented limits, together with the docs statement that the controller stops scaling up a bad ReplicaSet depending on maxUnavailable. [source] Course reasoning, labelled: the docs show a stuck rollout caused by an image pull error; the same mechanism applies when Pods never become ready.

Compare Recreate: all old Pods are killed before new ones are created, so there is downtime but never two versions at once. [source]

blocks.purpose: Show the stalled state of a default rollout with 3 replicas: surge is used up, unavailable is zero, so nothing more can move.
blocks.alt: Diagram of a rollout with 3 replicas, maxSurge 1 and maxUnavailable 0. On the left, the old ReplicaSet has 3 ready Pods. On the right, the new ReplicaSet has 1 Pod that is not ready. A bound shows total 4 equals replicas plus surge, so no more new Pods can be created. Another bound shows available 3 equals replicas minus unavailable 0, so no old Pod can be removed. The rollout is stuck until the new Pod becomes ready.

blocks.title: From manifest to limits to a predicted rollout

steps.html:
spec:
  replicas: 10
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 3
      maxUnavailable: 2

Course manifest fragment (the 10/3/2 numbers also appear in the docs' proportional-scaling example, but the fragment itself is ours). [source]

steps.prompt: You change the image. Right after, how many new Pods can be created, and how many old ones removed?
steps.html: Old: up to 2 may become unavailable at once, so 8 remain available. New: the total may reach 13, so with 8 old Pods up to 5 new Pods can exist. An early state could be old 8, new 5 (total 13). Illustrative; the controller may choose different intermediate counts within the limits.

steps.prompt: The new Pods crash on start and are never ready. What state does the rollout stop in, and what is serving traffic?
steps.html: The available count is at the floor of 8 (the old Pods), so no more old Pods can be removed, and the total of 13 is at the ceiling (8 old + 5 new), so no more new Pods can be created. The rollout waits at 8 old available + 5 not-ready new; 8 of 10 desired capacity serves traffic. This follows the documented limits (course derivation).

blocks.result: Stall check: floor reached and no new Pod becoming available means no further progress. Capacity at the stall is exactly the floor.

blocks.instructions: Trace the default settings for 3 replicas, one decision at a time. This is a static trace of the course author's model, not a recording of a cluster. Answer each prediction before the state shows.
blocks.debrief: You should have noticed the pattern: create one new Pod (surge), wait until it is available, only then remove one old Pod. With zero unavailable allowed, an old Pod is never removed ahead of its replacement.

config.title: Default rollout of 3 replicas
config.code:
spec:
  replicas: 3
  strategy:
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 25%
      maxUnavailable: 25%

steps.title: Round up the surge
steps.html: 25% of 3 is 0.75, rounded up to 1. Ceiling is 4 Pods.

steps.title: Round down the unavailable
steps.html: Rounded down to 0: all 3 desired Pods must stay available.

predict.prompt: How many new Pods can the controller create right now?
options: 0, until an old Pod is removed
predict.explanation: The ceiling is 4 and there are 3 Pods, so exactly one new Pod can be created. No old Pod may be removed because zero may be unavailable.

steps.title: New Pod becomes ready

options: Remove 1 old Pod (4 available → 3, floor is 3)
predict.explanation: Available is 4, floor 3, so one old Pod may go. Creating another new Pod would exceed the ceiling of 4 until an old one is removed.

steps.html: Old drops to 2 ready, new gets a second Pod (total 4 again). Repeat until old is 0. In this model that takes three rounds.

steps.title: Stall case: new Pod never ready

predict.prompt: The new Pod never becomes ready. What can the controller do next?
options: Nothing more: ceiling and floor are both reached
Create more new Pods to find a good one
predict.explanation: Total is 4 (ceiling). Available is 3 (floor). Removing an old Pod would violate the floor; creating a new one the ceiling. The rollout waits.

steps.html: The service keeps serving from the 3 old Pods while the rollout waits. This is a stall, not an outage.

assumptions: Models the documented limits, not every internal controller step.
Pod readiness is assumed to be decided elsewhere (next lesson).
Illustrative states, not from a real cluster.

blocks.task: A Deployment has replicas: 5, maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0. (a) Ceiling and floor? (b) If the new Pod never becomes ready, how many Pods exist and how many serve traffic when the rollout stalls? (c) The same Deployment with maxUnavailable: 2 and maxSurge: 0: (a) and (b) again.
hints: Ceiling = replicas + surge; floor = replicas − unavailable.
A stall happens when you are at the limits and no new Pod is available.
With surge 0 the controller must remove old Pods before creating new ones.
rubric: (c) Ceiling 5, floor 3; at stall old 3 available + 2 new not ready, 3 serve traffic
blocks.solution: (a) 6 and 5. (b) 5 old ready + 1 new not ready = 6 Pods; 5 serve. (c) Ceiling 5, floor 3. The controller can remove 2 old Pods and create 2 new. If those never become ready: 3 old available + 2 not-ready new, so only 3 of 5 desired Pods serve traffic. Same defect, but with this setting the user sees reduced capacity.

blocks.task: You manage a service with replicas: 4 that cannot lose any capacity during a deploy but has room for 2 extra Pods in the cluster. Write the strategy block you would choose, the ceiling and floor it gives, and one cost of that choice.
rubric: Names a cost: needs spare capacity, slower or more resource use during rollout, or a stall if new Pods never become ready
blocks.model: strategy: {type: RollingUpdate, rollingUpdate: {maxSurge: 2, maxUnavailable: 0}}. Ceiling 4 + 2 = 6; floor 4 − 0 = 4. Cost: during the rollout you pay for up to 6 Pods, and a bad version stalls rather than failing fast: it never reduces capacity, but you need a progress deadline to notice it. (Surge 50% of 4 = 2 also works.)

blocks.html: First attempts count as performance; later attempts are practice.

questions.prompt: replicas: 8, maxSurge: 25%, maxUnavailable: 25%. What are the ceiling and floor?
questions.explanation: 25% of 8 = 2 exactly, so no rounding matters: ceiling 8 + 2 = 10, floor 8 − 2 = 6.

feedback.1: That floor would mean unavailable 1; 25% of 8 is 2.

questions.prompt: replicas: 6, maxUnavailable: 25%. What is the largest number of Pods that may be unavailable? (Percentages round down.)
questions.feedbackWrong: Remember that maxUnavailable percentages round down, while maxSurge percentages round up.

questions.prompt: A rollout of 4 replicas with maxSurge 1 and maxUnavailable 0 has one new Pod that never becomes ready. Which is true?
options: The controller removes an old Pod anyway after some time
All 4 old Pods keep serving and the rollout waits
questions.explanation: The floor is 4 available, reached by the old Pods; the ceiling 5 is reached by the extra new Pod. No legal move exists, so the rollout waits while old Pods serve.

feedback.0: That would violate maxUnavailable: 0; the controller does not do that.
feedback.2: The old Pods remain available; capacity has not dropped.

questions.prompt: In your own words: why is "maxUnavailable: 0" safer for capacity but not a guarantee of a successful deploy?
rubric: Says old Pods are never removed ahead of ready replacements
Says a bad new version still stalls the rollout
Mentions detection (progress deadline) or a human fix
questions.model: With zero unavailable the controller only removes an old Pod after a replacement is available, so capacity never drops. But if new Pods never become ready the rollout simply waits; you still need to notice and fix or roll back.

blocks.task: New context: a batch-style worker Deployment with replicas: 2 uses the defaults (25% / 25%). A teammate says "that guarantees a smooth zero-downtime update". Compute the ceiling and floor, then explain whether the guarantee is justified, and what happens to the rollout if the new version is broken.
rubric: Identifies that zero may be unavailable
Explains a broken version stalls, with the old Pods still serving
Notes that zero downtime also depends on readiness being correct (next lesson)
blocks.model: Surge: ceil(0.5) = 1 so ceiling 3. Unavailable: floor(0.5) = 0 so floor 2. Old Pods are only removed once a new Pod is available, so a healthy update keeps 2 available. A broken version leaves 2 old Pods serving and 1 new unready Pod: a stalled rollout, not an outage. The guarantee depends on "available" being truthful, which depends on the readiness probe.

blocks.prompt: In your own words, write the two inequalities (ceiling and floor) a rolling update must respect, and describe how they cause a stalled rollout when the new Pods never become available.
